items.request:
Please polish this status update for my manager.

This week the fraud-scoring team finished the retraining run for model version 4.3 and moved it into shadow mode on Tuesday. Early numbers look encouraging: precision at the current review threshold is up about two points, though recall on card-not-present transactions barely moved, which we did not expect. Sofia traced part of that to a delay in the chargeback labels, so the newest fraud cases are still missing from the training window. We are going to rerun the evaluation once the labels land, probably Monday, and I would rather not promise a go-live date until then.

Meanwhile, Kenji is cleaning up the feature pipeline, which has been throwing intermittent timeouts since the storage upgrade. If that keeps happening, it could slow the shadow run, so I am watching it daily. I will send a fuller update after the rerun, and flag anything that changes the plan.

items.request:
Can you tighten this release note? It goes out with the 3.2 release.

Pipelinekit 3.2 release notes

- Faster setup
- Better alerts
- Smarter defaults

In this release, the init wizard now provisions a new project in about 4 minutes instead of the previous 25, mostly by caching the base container image. Alerts can now be routed per dataset to Slack or PagerDuty, and duplicate alerts within a 15-minute window are collapsed into one. Defaults for retry count and batch size are now picked from the last 30 days of run history for the same job type, replacing the fixed values of 3 and 500.

items.request:
Please polish this analysis note.

Analysis note: onboarding redesign (EXP-912)

We tracked weekly active users (WAU) for six weeks after launch. In the treatment arm, WAU rose from 41.2k to 44.9k, while the control group, which kept the old onboarding flow, stayed near 41k. The control group is a randomized comparison for this one experiment. The holdout group is different: it is a standing 5% slice of users excluded from every feature launch this quarter, so we can measure cumulative drift across all launches, not just this one. Weekly active users in the holdout group also drifted up, by about 0.8k, which suggests part of the lift in treatment is seasonal. We therefore report the WAU lift against the control group, and use the holdout group only as a sanity check on the overall trend. A follow-up on retention by cohort is planned for next sprint.

Our experimentation platform has changed how the product teams work this year. It's not a reporting tool, it's a decision engine. Before the platform, every launch debate turned into an argument over whose dashboard to trust. Now teams start from a shared set of metric definitions, and reviews move faster. Product managers tell us they now read experiment results before they read opinions.

The cultural shift matters as much as the tooling. It's not about running more tests, it's about asking sharper questions. Analysts now spend their time framing hypotheses with the people who own the roadmap. The platform team holds weekly office hours where anyone can bring a half-formed idea and leave with a testable design. It's not a gate for launches, it's a conversation starter.

You might think that a stricter review step would slow teams down, but the data shows median time from proposal to launch fell from 19 days to 12 days since we introduced it.

Looking ahead, the platform will keep growing with the teams that use it. It's not a finished product, it's a living system that improves with each experiment. We plan to extend it to the pricing and notifications groups next quarter. It's not just infrastructure, it's the way we learn.
